models.purpose: Rank artists by influence, separating direct from indirect, whole-network from within-genre, and breadth from depth.
models.summary: Katz centrality on the directed influence network, with the constant term replaced by the network order, then rescaled by an exponential of the negated centrality over years since the artist's decade. Four scores plus genre entropy form an influence vector; a fifth component, direct centrality inside the sonic genre, is added later.

variables.definition: Katz centrality of an artist on a chosen network.
Attenuation of indirect influence; must stay below the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue.
Adjacency matrix of the directed influence network.
Number of artists in the network under consideration.
Katz centrality rescaled by years elapsed and by an exponential of its own negation.
Decade in which the artist first became active.
Entropy of an artist's followers across genres.
The stacked vector of centrality scores and entropy whose norm ranks an artist.

governing_equations.source_expression: K_{N,alpha}(v_i) = alpha * sum_{j in N} A_{ij} * K_{N,alpha}(v_j) + 1
governing_equations.purpose: Katz centrality with a unit constant so that artists with no followers still score.
Rescale centrality so that artists from different decades can be compared.

governing_equations.source_expression: S(v) = - sum_{g in G} (followers of v in g / |g|) * log(followers of v in g / |g|)
governing_equations.purpose: Measure how widely an artist's influence spreads across genres.
Stack the four influence scores into one vector.
Extend the vector with direct centrality inside the artist's sonic genre.

equation_status.reason: Equations (1) to (4) and (10) are printed and were read from the raster.

objectives: Produce a single ranking of artists that respects time, directness, genre, and breadth.
constraints: alpha must lie below the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of A.
Indirect centrality is omitted on genre subnetworks because they are too small.
The constant 1 in equation (1) is replaced by the network order so scores compare across networks.

details: A static linear system; no time state is integrated.
The decay is capped by the largest eigenvalue of the whole network.

parameter_estimation.method: alpha1 is set at 0.2 of the maximum and alpha2 at the maximum, by inspection of the two regimes in Figure 3. The substitution of the network order for 1 is admitted to rest on quality of results.

steps: Solve the Katz system on the full network.
Replace the additive constant by the network order.
Solve direct Katz on each genre subnetwork.
Compute genre entropy and stack the vector.
software: not named for the centrality; the later clustering uses scikit-learn
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The linear system is solved directly; no iteration criterion is stated.

assumptions: Indirect influence accumulates geometrically, though the prose also says exponentially.
An artist's first decade is their most influential point.
Every component of the vector counts equally.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The ranking is computable and reported, but nothing in the data can test whether the ranking is right, which the paper concedes.

models.computational_cost: One sparse linear solve per network and per genre subnetwork.
strengths: Separates direct from indirect influence and whole-network from within-genre influence.
The time rescaling stops older artists from winning purely by having had longer.
limitations: The exponential in equation (2) is of the negated centrality, so a larger Katz score produces a smaller time-scaled score and the ranking inverts.
The prose says alpha must be greater than the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue; stability requires it to be smaller.
Replacing the constant by the network order was judged by eye.
missing_details: No value is given for the largest eigenvalue.
The normalization that makes the four components equally weighted is described but not written out.

models.purpose: Measure how alike two artists sound and cut the whole catalogue into four groups defined only by sound.
models.summary: Eleven sonic variables, scaled to the unit interval, give each artist a point. Similarity is the reciprocal of one plus the Euclidean distance. K-means with four centres minimizes the mean squared distance to the nearest centre, and the adjusted Rand index compares the result with the established genres.

variables.definition: Similarity between two sonic points, equal to one for identical points.
Euclidean distance between two sonic points.
Manhattan distance, defined but not used for the clustering.
Mean squared distance from each sonic point to its nearest centre.
Rand index between two partitions.
Rand index corrected for chance.

governing_equations.purpose: Turn a distance into a similarity bounded by one.
State the Manhattan alternative, which is not then used.
The k-means objective, mean squared distance to the nearest centre.
Rand index of two partitions of the artists.
Correct the Rand index for agreement expected by chance.

equation_status.reason: Equations (5) to (9) are printed and were read from the raster.

objectives: Group artists by sound alone and measure how far that grouping sits from the established genres.
constraints: Eleven variables: explicit is dropped as a content judgement and key is dropped as non-linear.
All variables scaled to the unit interval.
Four clusters, chosen because that count also maximizes the adjusted Rand index.

details: The initial placement of the centres is left to the library default.
No boundary condition; the space is bounded only by the scaling.
Iteration stops when the centres and the assignments stop changing.

parameter_estimation.method: The cluster count is a tuned hyperparameter, selected as four because Figure 5 peaks there. No other parameter is estimated.

steps: Scale the eleven variables to the unit interval.
Assign each point to its nearest centre.
Compute the adjusted Rand index against the established genres.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The library default; no tolerance is stated.

assumptions: Every sonic variable counts equally, because any other weighting would be arbitrary.
Euclidean distance is a fair measure of sonic closeness in eleven dimensions.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: A neural network recovers the four sonic genres from the sonic variables at 52 percent against a 25 percent chance rate, and the adjusted Rand index against the established genres is 0.161.

validation_refs: Figure 5, adjusted Rand index against cluster count.
models.computational_cost: K-means on 5045 points in eleven dimensions, repeated for several cluster counts.
strengths: The groups are built without ever seeing the genre labels.
The cluster count is cross-checked against an independent index rather than only against the objective.
limitations: The paper's own weakness section concedes that the literature uses more refined similarity functions than plain Euclidean distance.
Manhattan distance is defined and then never used.
Eleven dimensions is exactly the regime where Euclidean distance is known to degrade, and the paper raises this without resolving it.
missing_details: The cosine similarity mentioned in the prose has no formula.
The expected Rand index in equation (9) is not computed explicitly.

models.purpose: Locate musical revolutions as large moves of a popularity-weighted sonic centroid, and name the artists responsible.
models.summary: Modularity scores a partition of the influence network. Sonic contagiousness is the reciprocal of the mean absolute difference of a sonic variable across all influence edges. Revolutions are the decades where a centroid jumps past a hand-set threshold, and revolutionaries are eligible artists ranked by direct centrality times sonic similarity to the centroid after the jump.

variables.definition: Directed modularity of a partition of the influence network.
Number of edges in the network.
Out-degree of an artist.
In-degree of an artist.
Reciprocal of the mean absolute sonic difference across influence edges.
Similarity handed over from the sonic model, used to rank revolutionaries.
Influence vector handed over from the centrality model.

governing_equations.source_expression: Q_P = 1/m * sum_{p in P} sum_{v,v' in p} [A_{v,v'} - k_v^out * k_v'^in / m]
Sonic contagiousness = (number of edges) / sum |x_influencer - x_follower|
governing_equations.purpose: Score how faithfully a sonic variable passes from influencer to follower.

equation_status.reason: Equations (11) and (12) are printed and were read from the raster. The centroid-change rule that defines a revolution is stated only in prose.

objectives: Find the decades where the sound of the mainstream or of a genre moved most, and name the artists behind each move.
constraints: A mainstream revolution needs a centroid jump above 3.0.
A sonic-genre revolution needs a jump above 4.0.
A mainstreaming revolution needs the similarity to the mainstream to rise by more than 0.2.
Revolutionaries must have begun their career in the decade of the revolution.

details: Centroids are recomputed per window; nothing carries over.
The three thresholds bound what counts as a revolution.
No equilibrium; the detector reads a difference between windows.

parameter_estimation.method: The thresholds 3.0, 4.0 and 0.2 were chosen by hand so that each series shows a few clear peaks.

steps: Compute the popularity-weighted centroid per decade.
Take the distance moved between consecutive decades.
Mark a revolution where the move exceeds the threshold.
Rank eligible artists by direct centrality times similarity to the later centroid.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No iteration; the thresholds are fixed in advance.

assumptions: A revolution is a large, fast move of the centroid rather than a slow drift.
The artist responsible is active in the decade of the move and sounds like what the genre became.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: There is no ground truth for a revolution. The paper compares its dates with journalism after the fact and concedes the comparison runs backwards.

validation_refs: Figure 8, change in similarity to the mainstream.
models.computational_cost: One pass over the songs per decade window, then a sort of the eligible artists.
strengths: The same centroid construction serves the mainstream, the established genres and the sonic genres.
The revolutionary ranking combines influence with sonic similarity rather than using either alone.
limitations: The thresholds were set to produce a few clear peaks, so the revolutions are partly chosen.
The historical matching starts from a found revolution and hunts for an explanation.
Revolutionaries for the three mainstreaming revolutions were never computed.
The 1990s rhythm-and-blues revolution is credited to two styles that are not in the data.
missing_details: The popularity weighting inside the centroid is described but not written as a formula.
No null model is given for the modularity, though 0.38 is called significant.

dependency_edges.handoff: The sonic genre of each artist supplies the subnetwork on which the fifth component of the influence vector is computed.
Direct centrality from the influence vector ranks the revolutionaries.
Musical similarity to the post-revolution centroid weights the revolutionary ranking.
